newsitem.title: USA: Michigan gets reprieve in school funding case.
newsitem.headline: Michigan gets reprieve in school funding case.

text.p: Michigan won some breathing room in a school lawsuit that could cost the state $500 million when the state Supreme Court on Thursday reversed itself and agreed to hear an appeal of the case.
On September 27, the state's high court denied the state's motion for leave to appeal a September 1995 state appeals court order in the 16-year-old lawsuit brought by 84 school districts.
On Thursday, following an appeal by Gov. John Engler, the supreme court changed its mind opening the door to an appeal by the state.

The appellate court's September 1995 order essentially found the state had not been meeting its constitutional requirment of funding its share of total education costs, particularly in the special education and driver's education areas, according to a Michigan Department of Management and Budget summary of the case. And the court ordered the state to pay the districts nearly $500 million.
A spokesman for the school districts involved in the so-called Durant case, expressed disappointment in the high court's decision to hear an appeal.

"It is astounding to us that the state continues to amass interest and expenses on this debt to the taxpayers by needlessly drawing out the litigation process," said John Schultz, superintendent of the Rochester Community School District, in a news release.

He added that the lack of state funding for mandated education programs has led to cuts in school programs, budget deficits and additional property tax milllages that would have not been necessary if the state had paid schools "what is required by law."
A spokesman for Engler was not available for comment.

The initial rejection of a supreme court appeal led the state to cap spending, enact a hiring freeze and eliminate some capital spending projects, according to Maureen McNulty, a spokesman for the state's budget office.

She added that other school districts besides the ones in the lawsuit have claims pending that could bring the total potential impact of the school funding issue on the state to an estimated $3.5 billion.
